title: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
summary: Reuse one block of layers many times to get depth without parameters: Universal Transformers and halting, Huginn's prelude-core-coda design, random-depth training, test-time loops, and the tradeoffs.
outcomes: Explain why a (k x L) looped model has k layers of parameters but kL layers of compute and depth
Compute ACT halting steps, remainders and mixing weights for a sequence of halting probabilities
Describe the prelude, core and coda design and why the input is re-injected at every iteration
Explain how random iteration counts and truncated backprop make training memory independent of depth
Choose when looping helps (reasoning over context) versus hurts (memorization, latency)

lessons.title: Depth without parameters: what looping a block buys

blocks.md:
A GPT is a stack of $L$ distinct transformer blocks. Each token's vector passes through every block once, so the number of blocks is also the number of sequential refinement steps the model can apply before it must predict. Call that number the model's **depth**.

Many reasoning problems are multi-step: add 32 numbers, follow a chain of 16 references, resolve `a=b, b=c, c=?`. A fixed-depth model gets a fixed number of steps. Today there are two standard ways to get more: add layers (more parameters, more memory, more data to fill them) or let the model write out intermediate steps as chain-of-thought tokens (needs reasoning demonstrations to train on and a long context to hold them).

A **looped transformer** offers a third way. Take a small block $f$ of $k$ layers and apply it $L$ times to the same hidden states, feeding each output back in as the next input. The weights are identical on every pass. Saunshi et al. (2025) write this model as $(k \otimes L)$: $k$ unique layers, looped $L$ times.

Unrolled, a $(k \otimes L)$ model is just a $kL$-layer transformer whose groups of $k$ layers are forced to share weights. So it has the **parameters** of a $k$-layer model but the **depth and compute** of a $kL$-layer model.

blocks.tex: f^{(L)} = \underbrace{f \circ f \circ \cdots \circ f}_{L \text{ times}}, \qquad \text{params} \propto k, \qquad \text{FLOPs per token} \propto kL
blocks.caption: A (k x L) looped model: one k-layer block applied L times. Parameter count follows k; compute and sequential depth follow kL.

blocks.title: Twelve distinct blocks versus one block looped twelve times

scenes.caption: A standard 12-layer model: each block has its own weights and is visited once. Depth 12, parameters of 12 blocks.
A (1 x 12) looped model keeps only one block. Its output is fed back as its own input.
Each pass applies the same weights again. The hidden state changes; the parameters do not.
After 12 passes the head reads the final state. Same depth and roughly the same FLOPs as the 12-layer stack, one twelfth of the block parameters.
Side by side: unrolled, the looped model is a 12-layer stack in which every block is a copy of f.

blocks.md: Concrete numbers. A GPT-2-small-shaped layer with width $d = 768$ has about $12d^2$ matrix weights ($4d^2$ in attention, $8d^2$ in the MLP; ignoring biases, norms and embeddings): $12 \times 768^2 = 7{,}077{,}888$, about 7.08M per layer. Twelve distinct layers hold 84.9M. A $(1 \otimes 12)$ model holds 7.08M, yet each token still goes through twelve layer applications, so its matrix-multiply FLOPs per token (about 2 per weight per application) are the same as the 12-layer model's.

blocks.prompt: Saunshi et al. trained models to add 32 three-digit numbers with no chain-of-thought. A 12-layer model scores 100%. A 1-layer model scores 0.0%. What does a 1-layer model looped 12 times score?
blocks.reveal:
**99.6%.** The same 1-layer block, applied 12 times, nearly matches the 12-layer model with one twelfth of its parameters. The 2-layer model looped 6 times scores 99.5% while the plain 2-layer model scores 38.8%.

The lesson the authors draw: this task needs **depth** (many sequential steps), not many parameters.

scenes.caption: Shallow non-looped models fail on 32 operands: 0.0%, 38.8% and 60.7% for 1, 2 and 3 layers (Saunshi et al. 2025, Table 1).
Loop each small model up to an effective depth of 12 and accuracy jumps to 99.6%, 99.5% and 96.6%, close to the 12-layer baseline. Parameter counts are unchanged.

blocks.md: The same pattern holds on Saunshi et al.'s synthetic grade-school math (i-GSM, answers modulo 7): the 8-layer model scores 73.2%, the 1-layer model 24.5%, and the 1-layer model looped 8 times 73.2%. On these problems, depth is the bottleneck and looping supplies depth cheaply.

Looping saves **parameters** (memory, communication), not **compute**. Every loop is another full pass through the block, and the passes are sequential, so a $(1 \otimes 12)$ model is about as slow per token as a 12-layer model. Looped models trade memory for depth, they do not make inference free.
A looped transformer decouples depth from parameter count. $(k \otimes L)$ has $k$ layers of parameters and $kL$ layers of sequential computation.

blocks.question: You convert a 12-layer model into a (1 x 12) looped model of the same width. Which statement is correct?
options: Parameters drop about 12x and per-token FLOPs drop about 12x
Parameters drop about 12x and per-token FLOPs stay about the same
Parameters stay the same and per-token FLOPs drop about 12x
Both stay the same because the unrolled graph is identical
blocks.explain: The looped model stores one block instead of twelve, so parameters drop about 12x. But each token still goes through twelve block applications, so FLOPs (and latency) are about the same. The unrolled graph has the same shape, but its weights are tied, which is exactly what removes the parameters.

blocks.question: On i-GSM, (1 x 8) scores 73.2%, (8 x 1) scores 73.2% and (1 x 1) scores 24.5%. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: Looping only helps because it adds parameters
The task is limited by memorized knowledge, so parameters matter most
The task mainly needs sequential depth; parameters beyond one layer add little here
Looped models are always as good as deep models on every task
blocks.explain: The looped model has the parameters of (1 x 1) but matches (8 x 1), so what the extra layers provided was depth, not capacity. That does not generalize to every task: later in the course you will see that knowledge-heavy tasks do need parameters.

lessons.title: Universal Transformers: recurrence over depth with a halting rule

blocks.md: The idea is older than modern LLMs. **Universal Transformers** (UT), by Dehghani, Gouws, Vinyals, Uszkoreit and Kaiser (2018; Google Brain, DeepMind and the University of Amsterdam), apply one transformer block recurrently. An RNN recurs over **positions** (token 1, then token 2). A UT recurs over **revisions**: at every step it refines the vectors of all positions in parallel, using the same weights each time.

Each UT step has two sub-steps. First, self-attention lets every position read every other position. Second, a **transition function** (a position-wise feed-forward network, or a separable convolution for some tasks) is applied to each position. Both the attention weights and the transition weights are tied across steps. Residual connections, dropout and layer normalization wrap each sub-step, as in the original transformer.

blocks.caption: One UT step. H^t holds one d-dimensional vector per position after step t. P^t adds a coordinate embedding.

blocks.md: Because the block is shared, it needs a way to know which step it is on. UT adds $P^t$, the sum of a sinusoidal **position** embedding (as in the original transformer) and a sinusoidal **timestep** embedding computed the same way for step $t$. Keep this in mind: the later recurrent-depth LLM deliberately does *not* tell its block the step number.

UT's second idea is **dynamic halting**: let each position decide how many steps it needs. It borrows **Adaptive Computation Time** (ACT) from Graves (2016). At each step $n$, a small sigmoid unit outputs a halting probability $h^n$ for each position. The position keeps running until the running sum reaches $1-\epsilon$ (Graves used $\epsilon = 0.01$). The leftover mass at the final step is the **remainder** $R$. The output is a weighted mix of the per-step states, with weights $h^1, \dots, h^{N-1}, R$. A position that halts early has its state copied forward unchanged while the others keep going.

blocks.tex: N = \min\Big\{n : \sum_{i=1}^{n} h^i \ge 1-\epsilon\Big\}, \qquad R = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} h^i, \qquad s = \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} h^i s^i + R\, s^N
blocks.caption: ACT halting (Graves 2016). The weights sum to 1. Training adds a ponder cost N + R, scaled by a small coefficient, to discourage needless steps.

blocks.title: ACT on three positions (epsilon = 0.01, halt at 0.99)

scenes.caption: Step 1. Halting probabilities are 0.995, 0.6 and 0.2. 'the' already crosses 0.99, so it halts after one step with remainder 1 (nothing was accumulated before).
Step 2. 'cat' outputs 0.5: 0.6 + 0.5 = 1.1 crosses 0.99, so it halts with remainder 1 - 0.6 = 0.4. 'the' is copied forward. 'sat' reaches 0.5.
Step 3. Only 'sat' is still running: 0.5 + 0.3 = 0.8, below the threshold.
Step 4. 'sat' adds 0.4: 1.2 crosses 0.99, so it halts with remainder 1 - 0.8 = 0.2. All positions have halted, so the loop stops.
Final mixing weights per step (each row sums to 1): 'the' uses 1 x step 1; 'cat' uses 0.6 and 0.4; 'sat' uses 0.2, 0.3, 0.3 and remainder 0.2. Ponder costs N + R are 2, 2.4 and 4.2.

blocks.prompt: UT with ACT was run on bAbI, a set of synthetic story-question tasks. Some questions need one supporting fact from the story, others two or three. Would you expect the average number of steps per position to differ between those task types?
blocks.reveal: Yes. The average ponder time was **2.3 +/- 0.8** steps for one-fact tasks, **3.1 +/- 1.1** for two-fact tasks and **3.8 +/- 2.2** for three-fact tasks. The model learned on its own to spend more refinement steps when more reasoning hops are required, and to halt early on irrelevant facts.

blocks.md:
Results that made the paper influential:

- **Translation.** On WMT14 English-German, UT base (fixed steps, no ACT) scored 28.9 BLEU versus 28.0 for Transformer base with the same parameter count. ACT marginally hurt on translation.
- **Length generalization.** Trained on copy, reverse and addition strings of length 40 and tested on length 400, UT beat both LSTMs and transformers by a wide margin, though it was still far from perfect.
- **LAMBADA.** UT with dynamic halting set a new state of the art. It averaged 8.2 steps, and fixed-step UTs with 8 or 9 steps did not match it, suggesting halting also acts as a regularizer.

The paper also shows that, under certain assumptions, a UT is Turing-complete, unlike a fixed-depth transformer.

blocks.title: Trained on length 40, tested on length 400

scenes.caption: Character accuracy on 400-symbol strings (Dehghani et al. 2018, Table 4). The shared, repeatable block generalizes much further past the training length.
Whole-sequence accuracy is much harsher: one wrong symbol fails the sequence. UT reaches 0.35, 0.46 and 0.02; addition stays mostly unsolved.

blocks.md: Dynamic halting is not free accuracy. It helped on bAbI and LAMBADA but slightly hurt translation, adds a ponder-cost hyperparameter, and makes different positions in a batch finish at different times.

blocks.question: A position's halting unit outputs 0.3, 0.5, 0.4 at steps 1 to 3, with epsilon = 0.01. When does it halt and what is its remainder?
options: Step 2, remainder 0.2
Step 3, remainder 0.2
Step 3, remainder 0.4
It never halts because the sum never equals exactly 0.99
blocks.explain: Running sums are 0.3, 0.8, 1.2. The first to reach 0.99 is step 3, so N = 3. The remainder is 1 minus the sum before the halting step: 1 - 0.8 = 0.2. The step-3 halting probability (0.4) is replaced by the remainder so the weights sum to 1.

blocks.question: Which parameters does a Universal Transformer share across its recurrent steps?
options: Only the feed-forward transition; each step has its own attention
Only the attention; each step has its own transition
Both the self-attention and the transition function
Nothing; it shares weights across positions only, like any transformer
blocks.explain: In UT both the self-attention and transition weights are tied across steps, which is what makes the number of steps changeable. (Every transformer already shares weights across positions; that is not what makes UT recurrent.)

lessons.title: Recurrent depth at scale: prelude, core block and coda

blocks.md: In 2025, Geiping, McLeish, Jain, Kirchenbauer, Singh, Bartoldson, Kailkhura, Bhatele and Goldstein (ELLIS Tuebingen, University of Maryland, LLNL) scaled a depth-recurrent decoder to 3.5B parameters and about 800B tokens on the Frontier supercomputer. The released model is **Huginn-0125**. The goal: scale test-time compute by thinking in the continuous hidden space, instead of by generating more chain-of-thought tokens.

The model has three groups of standard causal decoder layers:

- **Prelude** $P$: embeds tokens and runs a few layers to produce $\mathbf{e}$, a latent encoding of the input.
- **Core recurrent block** $R$: the looped part. It takes the current state $\mathbf{s}_{i-1}$ *and* $\mathbf{e}$ and returns $\mathbf{s}_i$.
- **Coda** $C$: a few layers plus the tied output head that turn the final state into next-token probabilities.

The starting state is random noise, and the loop count $r$ can be chosen freely on every forward pass.

blocks.caption: The recurrent-depth forward pass (Geiping et al. 2025, Section 3.1). States have shape n x h: one h-dimensional vector per token.

blocks.title: One forward pass of a recurrent-depth model

nodes.label:
Adapter A
concat(s, e) to h

scenes.caption: The prelude runs once per token and produces e. It never loops.
The state starts as random noise, not as e. Starting from noise pushes the model toward a result that does not depend on where the state began.
Iteration 1: the adapter concatenates s and e (2h features) and maps them back to h, then the 4 core layers update the state.
Each further iteration feeds s_i back with the same e. Same weights every time; only the state changes.
After r iterations, the coda reads s_r and predicts the next token. r = 32 gives 2 + 4 x 32 + 2 = 132 effective layers.

blocks.md:
Why re-inject $\mathbf{e}$ at every step? The authors use gradient descent as the analogy: to minimize a function of variable $\mathbf{x}$ and data $\mathbf{y}$, every step uses $\mathbf{y}$. If the data were only given at the start (say $\mathbf{s}_0 = \mathbf{e}$), the iteration's end point would depend only on that starting point, and the loop could not act like a stable optimizer over the input.

They also tried two alternatives: adding fresh noise at every step (did not help), and giving the core block the current step number (as UT's timestep embedding does). The step-aware block hurt **path independence** (converging to the same answer regardless of the start) and produced models that could not extrapolate to more iterations.

Inside each group, layers are standard: causal self-attention with RoPE (base 50000), a gated SiLU MLP and RMSNorm. To keep the recurrence stable at scale, every layer uses a **sandwich** norm layout: normalize the input of each sublayer *and* the output of each residual sum. The core block also ends with an RMSNorm, so the state handed to the next iteration has a controlled scale.

blocks.caption: The sandwich layer used in every block of Huginn. n_1 to n_4 are RMSNorms.

blocks.md:
The production shape is $(l_P, l_R, l_C) = (2, 4, 2)$ with width $h = 5280$ (55 heads of 96), MLP width 17920, a 65,536-token vocabulary and 4096-token sequences. The paper reports about 1.5B parameters in prelude plus coda, 1.5B in the core and 0.5B in the tied embedding. A quick check of the core: each layer has $4h^2 \approx 111.5$M attention weights plus $3 \times h \times 17920 \approx 283.9$M MLP weights, about 395M, and four layers give about 1.58B.

The model card's rule of thumb: running $r$ iterations behaves like **materializing $1.5r + 2$ billion parameters**. At $r = 32$ that is 50B, which is where the paper's "compute equivalent to 50B parameters" claim comes from.

blocks.title: Effective size grows linearly with the loop count

scenes.caption: Huginn's numbers: 1.5B core, 2B everything else. r = 32, the training mean, unrolls to about 50B parameters' worth of compute while only 3.5B are stored.
A smaller core (0.5B) still grows linearly, just with a shallower slope. Compute per token scales with core size x r, while memory for weights stays fixed.

blocks.prompt: Huginn was trained with a random number of iterations averaging about 32. If you run the final model with r = 1, how does it do compared with r = 32?
blocks.reveal:
It collapses. On GSM8K with chain-of-thought prompting, r = 32 scores 34.8 to 42.1% (depending on the answer-matching rule) while r = 1 scores 0.0. ARC-Easy drops from 69.9 to 34.9.

The authors also note that r = 1 barely improved between the 180B-token and 800B-token checkpoints: the later gains live in the iterations of the core block, not in the prelude or coda.

blocks.title: Same data, same setup: recurrent versus fixed depth (Table 4)

scenes.caption: ARC-Challenge. At 180B tokens the recurrent model at r = 32 beats its fixed-depth twin (29.2 vs 27.0). At r = 1 it is near chance (23.7). By 800B tokens r = 32 reaches 38.2.
HellaSwag shows the same shape: 37.3 fixed, 48.8 recurrent at r = 32 after 180B tokens, 65.2 after 800B. With one iteration the model is near chance either way.
SciQ (fact recall): 80.6 vs 73.2 at 180B. Measured above chance (25), that is a 1.15x gain versus 2.1x on ARC-Challenge and 5x on GSM8K, so the paper calls the two models more similar here.

blocks.md: Getting there was not smooth. The first large run used parameter-free norms, no embedding scale and a plain additive adapter $A(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{e}) = \mathbf{s} + \mathbf{e}$. It stalled: the hidden states of all tokens became almost perfectly correlated (**representation collapse**), because each iteration mixed the sequence a bit more. The second run (pre-norm, learned adapter) recovered from collapse but learned to **ignore the incoming state**: validation perplexity was the same at 1 and 32 iterations. The third run, with the sandwich layout and a lower learning rate, trained smoothly and kept improving with more iterations.

A looped model can quietly stop using its loop. If it learns to ignore $\mathbf{s}$, extra iterations do nothing. Track validation loss at several iteration counts (Huginn tracked 1, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64) during training, not just at the default.

blocks.question: A colleague simplifies the design: set s0 = e and stop feeding e into later iterations. What does the paper's reasoning predict?
options: Nothing changes, because e is already inside s0
The loop becomes less stable: its end point depends on the starting point, not on continued use of the input
Training becomes cheaper and generalizes better because the adapter is removed
The model becomes a Universal Transformer and gains Turing completeness
blocks.explain: The authors argue the input must be injected at every step, as data enters every step of gradient descent. With e only in the initial state, the iteration cannot behave like a stable, input-dependent operator; its result depends on the boundary condition.

blocks.question: Using the model card's rule (materialized params = 1.5r + 2 billion), what does running Huginn at r = 16 correspond to, and how many effective layers is that?
options: 26B and 68 layers
24B and 64 layers
26B and 64 layers
50B and 132 layers
blocks.explain: 1.5 x 16 + 2 = 26 billion. Effective depth is 2 prelude + 4 x 16 core + 2 coda = 68 layers. 50B and 132 layers is the r = 32 point.

lessons.title: Training for any loop count: random depth and truncated backprop

blocks.md: If you always train with $r = 32$, the model learns to be good at exactly 32 iterations, and running it with 64 at test time is out of distribution. Geiping et al. instead sample a **random iteration count for every training sequence** and minimize the expected loss over both data and iteration counts. This trains one set of weights that works across a range of depths.

blocks.caption: x' is the sequence shifted left (the next tokens). Lambda is the distribution of iteration counts.

blocks.md: The distribution $\Lambda$ is a **log-normal Poisson**: draw a log-rate from a normal, then draw a Poisson count with that rate, then add 1 so $r \ge 1$. With target mean $\bar r = 32$ and $\sigma = 1/2$, the mean of $r$ is $\bar r + 1 = 33$. Most draws are below 32, with a heavy tail of occasional long runs.

blocks.caption: The minus sigma^2/2 term makes the log-normal rate have mean r-bar exactly.

blocks.title: Iteration counts sampled during training (2 million simulated draws)

scenes.caption: Share of training sequences per bucket of r, from our simulation of the paper's sampler (r-bar = 32, sigma = 0.5). The 17-32 range holds about 44% of draws.
The skew: the median is 29 and 55.8% of draws are below 32, yet 5.8% exceed 64 and the 99th percentile is 94. The model regularly sees much deeper unrolls than average.

blocks.md:
A heavy tail creates a memory problem: backpropagating through 94 iterations would store activations for all 94. The fix is **truncated backpropagation**: run all but the last $k$ iterations under `no_grad` and backpropagate only through the last $k$. Huginn fixes $k = 8$. Activation memory and backward compute are now bounded by $k$, independent of how large $r$ is.

The prelude still learns every step, because its output $\mathbf{e}$ is injected into each of the last $k$ iterations, so gradient flows back to it through all of them. This mirrors truncated backpropagation through time for RNNs, applied to depth instead of time.

blocks.title: The training-time sampler and loop (simplified from the released code)
blocks.code:
import math, torch

def sample_iterations(mean=32, k=8, sigma=0.5):
    mu = math.log(mean) - sigma**2 / 2
    rate = math.exp(torch.normal(mu, sigma, (1,)).item())
    p = torch.poisson(torch.tensor(rate)).item() + 1
    n_no_grad = max(p - k, 0)   # iterations without gradient
    n_grad = min(k, p)          # last k iterations keep gradients
    return int(n_no_grad), int(n_grad)

def forward(x, model):
    e = model.prelude(x)                  # gets gradients
    s = model.random_state_like(e)
    n_no_grad, n_grad = sample_iterations()
    with torch.no_grad():
        for _ in range(n_no_grad):
            s = model.core(model.adapter(torch.cat([s, e], -1)))
    for _ in range(n_grad):
        s = model.core(model.adapter(torch.cat([s, e], -1)))
    return model.coda(s)                  # loss on next tokens

scenes.caption: Start of a training step: run the prelude once to get e. This part always receives gradients.
The state starts as random noise shaped like e.
Sample the depth. mu = ln 32 - 0.125 = 3.341. Suppose the normal draw gives a rate of 19.4 and the Poisson draw gives 19.
Split p = 20 into 12 iterations without gradient and the last 8 with gradient.
The first 12 iterations run under no_grad: no activations are stored for backward. They just move the state forward.
The last 8 iterations record the graph. Backward will run through these 8 and, via e, into the prelude.
Had the draw been p = 3, there would be 0 no-grad and 3 grad iterations; for p = 70, 62 and 8. Stored activations never exceed 8 iterations.
The coda reads the final state and the loss compares against the next tokens.

blocks.title: Work per training step at three sampled depths (simplified)

scenes.caption: r = 3: all three iterations keep gradients. Assuming backward costs about 2x forward (a common rule of thumb), backward takes 6 core-pass units.
r = 20: 12 cheap no-grad iterations, then 8 recorded ones. Backward covers only the 8 recorded iterations: 16 units.
r = 70 (a tail draw): forward work grows to 70 passes, but the recorded part and backward stay at 8 iterations. Memory per step is the same as for r = 20.

blocks.md:
Two systems details follow from this design.

- **Locked-step sampling.** With thousands of data-parallel workers, each drawing its own $r$, everyone would wait for the worker with the deepest unroll. Huginn samples one $r$ per micro-batch and synchronizes it across workers.
- **More FLOPs per parameter.** Because weights are shared, even the 3.5B model fit with plain data parallelism plus optimizer-state sharding, no tensor parallelism. The paper reports 52 to 64 TFLOP/s per GPU (41 to 51% of achievable) on 4096 AMD MI250X GPUs, with a global batch of 16M tokens per step.

Random iteration counts teach one set of weights to work at many depths. Truncated backprop through only the last $k$ iterations keeps training memory independent of $r$, while the input injection still sends gradient to the prelude.

blocks.question: With k = 8, a training step happens to draw r = 100 instead of r = 20. What happens to activation memory for the core block?
options: It grows about 5x, because there are 5x more iterations
It stays about the same, because only the last 8 iterations are recorded
It drops, because the no-grad iterations free memory used by earlier steps
Training crashes, because the sampler is clamped to at most 64
blocks.explain: Only the last k = 8 iterations build the autograd graph, so stored activations are bounded by 8 iterations regardless of r. Forward compute does grow with r (100 passes instead of 20). The sampler has no clamp; tail draws above 64 happen about 5.8% of the time.

blocks.question: Gradients flow only through the last 8 core iterations. Why does the prelude still get trained on every step?
options: It does not; the prelude is frozen after warm-up
Because the coda shares weights with the prelude
Because the no-grad iterations are re-run with gradients at the end of the step
Because e is injected into every iteration, including the last 8, so gradients reach the prelude through each of them
blocks.explain: The adapter concatenates s and e at every iteration. During the last k recorded iterations, the loss depends on e through k paths, so the prelude receives gradient from all of them. Only the tied embedding is shared between input and output head, not the prelude layers.

lessons.title: Spending compute at test time: more loops, early exits, shared caches

blocks.md: At inference you choose $r$ with an argument (`num_steps` in the released Hugging Face code). More iterations mean more compute per token and, up to a point, better answers. The model card's guidance: fewer than 4 steps gives very coarse answers, benchmarks keep improving up to around 64 steps when there is enough context to reason about, and beyond that more steps generally neither help nor hurt.

blocks.title: Accuracy as test-time iterations grow (Huginn, zero-shot)

scenes.caption: r = 4: the model is weak across the board (Geiping et al. 2025, Table 1).
r = 8: big jumps everywhere. HellaSwag goes from 43.5 to 58.5.
r = 16: still improving, notably MMLU (25.3 to 31.3).
r = 32: most of these zero-shot tasks have nearly saturated. Harder tasks with more context (math, few-shot ARC) keep using extra iterations longer.

blocks.md: How many iterations a task can use depends on the task and on the context. HellaSwag reaches near peak at about 8 iterations, while GSM8K and HumanEval keep improving further. On ARC-Challenge with no few-shot examples, accuracy saturates around 8 to 12 iterations; with 1 example around 20; with 25 to 50 examples around 32. More context gives the model more to reason about, so it uses more depth.

Fixed $r$ wastes compute on easy tokens. A recurrent-depth model gives you **per-token early exit** without any special training: iterate until the prediction stops changing. Huginn's criterion: compute the next-token distribution after each iteration and stop when the KL divergence between two successive steps falls below $5 \times 10^{-4}$, then sample and move to the next token. Standard transformers need models trained specifically for early exits or extra exit heads for this.

blocks.tex: \text{stop at the first } i \text{ with } \mathrm{KL}\big(p_{i-1} \,\|\, p_i\big) < 5 \times 10^{-4}
blocks.caption: p_i is the coda's next-token distribution after iteration i. The released code also offers entropy-, latent- and argmax-stability-based rules.

blocks.title: Toy early exit: the prediction settles, the KL drops, the loop stops

scenes.caption: Simplified toy (not Huginn): 4 logits updated by s_i = 0.5 s_(i-1) + e, which converges to 2e. After step 1 the distribution is 0.394 / 0.375 / 0.138 / 0.093.
Step 2: A pulls ahead (0.490). KL to step 1 is 2.24e-2, far above 5e-4, so keep going.
Step 3: KL = 5.21e-3. Still above the threshold.
Step 4: KL = 1.25e-3. Close, but still above.
Step 5: KL = 3.05e-4 < 5e-4, so exit. Running to step 12 would barely change anything (0.584 / 0.263 / 0.118 / 0.036): 7 iterations saved.

blocks.md: Evidence that this works zero-shot: on the first 50 questions from several MMLU categories, the number of iterations before exit varied by subject; the model exited earliest on high school mathematics and took on average 3.5 more steps on moral scenarios. On MT-Bench, early exits scored 5.56 versus 5.66 with a fixed 32 iterations, a difference well inside the standard error of about 0.39.

Early exit creates a **KV-cache** puzzle. Every iteration of every core layer writes its own keys and values for each token, so the cache has one entry per token per iteration (the released code needs its own cache class for this). If an earlier token exited at iteration 7, a later token at iteration 20 finds no entry at depth 20. Huginn's answer: attend to the **latest, deepest available** entry. Because every iteration uses the same K and V projection matrices on successive states, those entries are compatible.

The same property enables **KV-cache sharing**: give each token a fixed budget of $k$ cache slots for the recurrence, and at iteration $i$ read and write slot $i \bmod k$. With a budget of 16, iteration 17 overwrites iteration 1's slot. With a budget of 4, MT-Bench scored 5.86, no loss. (The released code counts this budget in core-layer cache entries: `compress-s16` keeps 16 entries per token, which is the last 4 iterations of the 4-layer core.)

blocks.title: KV-cache sharing for one token and one core layer (budget k = 4)

scenes.caption: Iterations 1 to 4 write slots 1, 2, 3, 0 (i mod 4). The cache is full.
Iteration 5 maps to slot 1 and overwrites iteration 1's keys and values.
After iteration 8 the cache holds the 4 most recent iterations: 8, 5, 6, 7.

After iteration 10: slots hold 8, 9, 10, 7. Reading the budget as 4 iterations of the 4-layer core, with r = 32 the cache per token drops from 4 + 4 x 32 = 132 layer entries to 4 + 4 x 4 = 20, a 6.6x saving.

blocks.md:
Two more tricks fall out of the architecture:

- **Continuous chain-of-thought.** Instead of starting each new token's recurrence from noise, warm-start it from the previous token's final state $\mathbf{s}_r$. The paper reports this cuts the average steps to converge by 1 to 2; its Figure 10 means drop by 0.2 to 1.2 steps across four MMLU categories.
- **Self-speculative decoding.** Draft several tokens with few iterations, then verify them with more iterations. The draft model is the same model, and drafting states can be reused during verification.

Per-token early exit saves FLOPs per token, but in batched serving tokens that exit early may sit idle waiting for others. Relaxed Recursive Transformers (Bae et al. 2024) propose **continuous depth-wise batching**, scheduling new work into slots freed by early exits; their simulation estimates 2 to 3x throughput, not a measured deployment.

blocks.question: Successive-step KL values for one token are 2.24e-2, 5.21e-3, 1.25e-3, 3.05e-4, 7.52e-5 (measured after steps 2 to 6). With Huginn's threshold of 5e-4, after which step does the token exit?
options: Step 4
Step 6
Step 5
It never exits; KL must reach exactly 0
blocks.explain: The first value below 5e-4 is 3.05e-4, measured between steps 4 and 5, so the token exits after step 5. 1.25e-3 (step 4) is still above the threshold.

blocks.question: Huginn runs with a KV budget of 16 slots per token. Which slot does iteration 33 write, and whose entry does it replace?
options: Slot 1, replacing iteration 17
Slot 0, replacing iteration 32
Slot 1, replacing iteration 1 only
Slot 33, because each iteration gets a new slot
blocks.explain: 33 mod 16 = 1. Slot 1 was written by iteration 1, overwritten by iteration 17, and is now overwritten by iteration 33. It works because all iterations use the same K and V projections, so entries from different depths are compatible.

lessons.title: When looping helps, when it hurts, and the design space

blocks.md: Looping gives depth without parameters. What does it lose? Saunshi, Dikkala, Li, Kumar and Reddi (Google Research, 2025) pretrained 1B-scale language models on 250B tokens of the Pile and compared, for each budget $k$: the 24-layer baseline $(24 \otimes 1)$, a $k$-layer model $(k \otimes 1)$ with the same parameters as the looped one, and the looped model $(k \otimes 24/k)$ with the depth and FLOPs of the baseline. They grouped downstream tasks into closed-book QA (memorization), open-book QA, math word problems and reasoning primitives.

To compare groups, they define **% Gap**: how much of the distance between the small model and the full baseline the looped model closes. 0% means looping did nothing (parameters are what matter); 100% means looping fully replaces the missing parameters; above 100% means the looped model beats the full baseline.

blocks.caption: Avg_G is the average score of a task group G (Saunshi et al. 2025, Eq. 1).

blocks.title: 6 layers, 6 layers looped 4x, and 24 layers (Saunshi et al. Table 3)

scenes.caption: Closed-book QA (memorization): 11.2 / 4.0 / 8.2. Looping recovers only 58% of the gap; parameters matter for stored facts.
Open-book QA (answer is in the context): 33.9 / 19.3 / 28.7, closing 64% of the gap.
Math word problems: 29.3 / 17.7 / 29.8. The looped model matches the 24-layer one with a quarter of the parameters: (29.8 - 17.7) / (29.3 - 17.7) = 104%.
Reasoning primitives (variable-assignment chains): 47.5 / 24.1 / 56.1. The looped model clearly beats the full baseline, a gap above 130%.
Validation perplexity (lower is better): 7.40 / 9.25 / 8.42. Looping closes only about 44% of the perplexity gap, so perplexity alone undersells looped models on reasoning.

blocks.md: Huginn shows the same split. On OpenBookQA in the normal closed-book format it scores 38.2, below OLMo-2's 46.2. When the relevant fact is provided in the prompt, it jumps to 49.2 (+11.0), close to OLMo-2's 53.4. The authors' reading: the recurrent model has less capacity to memorize facts but more capacity to reason about its context. A related 2025 effort, Ouro (Zhu et al.), reports the same theme from controlled experiments: its looped models' advantage comes from better knowledge manipulation, not more knowledge capacity.

Looping buys **depth** (multi-step reasoning, using context), not **capacity** (memorized facts). Judge a looped model on reasoning tasks at matched FLOPs, not only on perplexity at matched parameters.

The other costs are the ones from lesson 1, now with Huginn's numbers. Each token passes through $4 + 4r$ layers: 20 at $r = 4$, 132 at $r = 32$, 260 at $r = 64$. These passes are sequential, so latency grows linearly with $r$. Without sharing, the KV cache also grows with $r$. And training is touchier: the representation-collapse and ignored-state failures from lesson 3 were real at scale.

blocks.title: The design space of looped transformers

scenes.caption: Axis 1, what to share. UT loops the whole block stack; ALBERT shares parameters across all its layers to shrink BERT.
Axis 2, where to loop. Middle looping keeps unique first and last layers and loops the middle (Saunshi et al.; MoR's Middle-Cycle; Huginn's prelude and coda).
Axis 3, from scratch or converted. Relaxed Recursive Transformers initialize a shared block from a pretrained model (e.g. Gemma 2B to a recursive 1B) and add a small LoRA per loop to relax the tying.
Axis 4, how many loops per token. ACT halting (UT), a KL exit rule (Huginn), a learned router (MoR), or an entropy-regularized learned exit (Ouro).

blocks.md:
Two recent designs in more detail:

- **Mixture-of-Recursions** (Bae et al. 2025) adds lightweight routers that assign each token its own recursion depth. In expert-choice routing each recursion step keeps its top-$k$ tokens; in token-choice routing each token commits to a depth up front. For the cache, it either stores KV only for tokens active at each depth, or computes KV once at the first recursion and reuses it in later ones. It was tested from 135M to 1.7B parameters.
- **Ouro** (2025) pretrains looped language models on 7.7T tokens with an entropy-regularized objective that learns how much depth to use; its 1.4B and 2.6B models are reported to match results of up to 12B models on many benchmarks.

blocks.question: You must ship a small on-device model mainly for trivia-style factual QA with no retrieval. Memory is tight, latency matters. Is a looped model a good fit?
options: Yes: looping recovers the full accuracy of a 4x larger model on any task
Not really: closed-book QA depends on stored knowledge, which looping recovers poorly, and every loop adds latency
Yes: looping lowers latency because the weights stay in cache
No: looped models cannot be quantized
blocks.explain: Closed-book QA is the task group where looping closed the least of the gap (58% for k = 6) because it depends on capacity. Loops also add sequential compute. Looping shines on reasoning over context; adding retrieval (moving facts into the context) is the setting where a looped model does better.

blocks.question: For k = 8, Saunshi et al. report open-book QA scores of 33.9 (24 layers), 22.7 (8 layers) and 30.8 (8 layers looped 3x). What is the % Gap?
options: About 24%
About 51%
About 72%
About 136%
blocks.explain: (30.8 - 22.7) / (33.9 - 22.7) = 8.1 / 11.2 = 0.72, about 72%, matching the paper's table. The looped model recovers most of the missing parameters' benefit on this context-reasoning group.
